courses.prerequisite_text: graduate standing. Nongraduate students may enroll with consent of instructor.

courses.title: Seminar in Computational and Applied Mathematics
courses.description: Various topics in computational and applied mathematics.
courses.prerequisite_text: graduate standing. Nongraduate students may enroll with consent of instructor. (S/U grade only.)

courses.title: Seminar in Mathematics of Information, Data, and Signals
courses.description: Various topics in the mathematics of information, data, and signals.
courses.prerequisite_text: graduate standing or consent of instructor. (S/U grade only.)

courses.title: Seminar in Optimization
courses.description: Various topics in optimization and applications. May be taken for credit nine times.
courses.prerequisite_text: graduate standing. (S/U grade only.)

courses.title: Projects in Computational and Applied Mathematics
courses.description: (Conjoined with MATH 179.) Mathematical models of physical systems arising in science and engineering, good models and well-posedness, numerical and other approximation techniques, solution algorithms for linear and nonlinear approximation problems, scientific visualizations, scientific software design and engineering, project-oriented. Graduate students will do an extra paper, project, or presentation per instructor.
courses.prerequisite_text: MATH 174, or MATH 274, or consent of instructor.

courses.title: Probability Theory I
courses.description: This is the first course in a three-course sequence in probability theory. Topics covered in the sequence include the measure-theoretic foundations of probability theory, independence, the Law of Large Numbers, convergence in distribution, the Central Limit Theorem, conditional expectation, martingales, Markov processes, and Brownian motion. Recommended preparation: completion of real analysis equivalent to MATH 140A-B strongly recommended.
courses.prerequisite_text: graduate standing.

courses.title: Probability Theory II
courses.description: This is the second course in a three-course sequence in probability theory. Topics covered in the sequence include the measure-theoretic foundations of probability theory, independence, the Law of Large Numbers, convergence in distribution, the Central Limit Theorem, conditional expectation, martingales, Markov processes, and Brownian motion.
courses.prerequisite_text: a grade of B or better required in MATH 280A. Students who have not completed MATH 280A may enroll with consent of instructor.

courses.title: Probability Theory III
courses.description: This is the third course in a three-course sequence in probability theory. Topics covered in the sequence include the measure-theoretic foundations of probability theory, independence, the Law of Large Numbers, convergence in distribution, the Central Limit Theorem, conditional expectation, martingales, Markov processes, and Brownian motion.
courses.prerequisite_text: a grade of B or better required in MATH 280B. Students who have not completed MATH 280B may enroll with consent of instructor.

courses.title: Mathematical Statistics
courses.description: Statistical models, sufficiency, efficiency, optimal estimation, least squares and maximum likelihood, large sample theory.
courses.prerequisite_text: advanced calculus and basic probability theory or consent of instructor.

courses.title: Mathematical Statistics
courses.description: Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals, one-sample and two-sample problems. Bayes theory, statistical decision theory, linear models and regression.
courses.prerequisite_text: advanced calculus and basic probability theory or consent of instructor.

courses.title: Mathematical Statistics
courses.description: Nonparametrics: tests, regression, density estimation, bootstrap and jackknife. Introduction to statistical computing using S plus.
courses.prerequisite_text: advanced calculus and basic probability theory or consent of instructor.

courses.title: Applied Statistics I
courses.description: General theory of linear models with applications to regression analysis. Ordinary and generalized least squares estimators and their properties. Hypothesis testing, including analysis of variance, and confidence intervals. Completion of courses in linear algebra and basic statistics are recommended prior to enrollment.
courses.prerequisite_text: graduate standing or consent of instructor. (S/U grades permitted.)

courses.title: Applied Statistics II
courses.description: Diagnostics, outlier detection, robust regression. Variable selection, ridge regression, the lasso. Generalized linear models, including logistic regression. Data analysis using the statistical software R. Students who have not taken MATH 282A may enroll with consent of instructor.
courses.prerequisite_text: MATH 282A or consent of instructor. (S/U grades permitted.)

courses.title: Statistical Methods in Bioinformatics
courses.description: This course will cover material related to the analysis of modern genomic data; sequence analysis, gene expression/functional genomics analysis, and gene mapping/applied population genetics. The course will focus on statistical modeling and inference issues and not on database mining techniques.
courses.prerequisite_text: one year of calculus, one statistics course or consent of instructor.

courses.title: Lifetime Data Analysis
courses.description: Survival analysis is an important tool in many areas of applications including biomedicine, economics, engineering. It deals with the analysis of time to events data with censoring. This course discusses the concepts and theories associated with survival data and censoring, comparing survival distributions, proportional hazards regression, nonparametric tests, competing risk models, and frailty models. The emphasis is on semiparametric inference, and material is drawn from recent literature. Students who have not completed listed prerequisites may enroll with consent of instructor.
courses.prerequisite_text: MATH 282A. Students who have not completed listed prerequisite may enroll with consent of instructor.

courses.title: Stochastic Processes
courses.description: Elements of stochastic processes, Markov chains, hidden Markov models, martingales, Brownian motion, Gaussian processes. Recommended preparation: completion of undergraduate probability theory (equivalent to MATH 180A) highly recommended.
courses.prerequisite_text: graduate standing. Nongraduate students may enroll with consent of instructor.

courses.title: Stochastic Differential Equations
courses.description: Review of continuous martingale theory. Stochastic integration for continuous semimartingales. Existence and uniqueness theory for stochastic differential equations. Strong Markov property. Selected applications.
courses.prerequisite_text: MATH 280A-B or consent of instructor.

courses.title: Time Series Analysis
courses.description: Discussion of finite parameter schemes in the Gaussian and non-Gaussian context. Estimation for finite parameter schemes. Stationary processes and their spectral representation. Spectral estimation. Students who have not taken MATH 282A may enroll with consent of instructor.
courses.prerequisite_text: MATH 282A or consent of instructor.

courses.title: Multivariate Analysis
courses.description: Bivariate and more general multivariate normal distribution. Study of tests based on Hotelling’s T2. Principal components, canonical correlations, and factor analysis will be discussed as well as some competing nonparametric methods, such as cluster analysis. Students who have not taken MATH 282A may enroll with consent of instructor.
courses.prerequisite_text: MATH 282A or consent of instructor.

courses.title: Advanced Time Series Analysis
courses.description: Nonparametric function (spectrum, density, regression) estimation from time series data. Nonlinear time series models (threshold AR, ARCH, GARCH, etc.). Nonparametric forms of ARMA and GARCH. Multivariate time series. Students who have not taken MATH 287A may enroll with consent of instructor.
courses.prerequisite_text: MATH 287A or consent of instructor.

courses.title: Statistical Learning
courses.description: Topics include regression methods: (penalized) linear regression and kernel smoothing; classification methods: logistic regression and support vector machines; model selection; and mathematical tools and concepts useful for theoretical results such as VC dimension, concentration of measure, and empirical processes. Students who have not taken MATH 282A may enroll with consent of instructor.
courses.prerequisite_text: MATH 282A or consent of instructor.

courses.title: Seminar in Probability and Statistics
courses.description: Various topics in probability and statistics.
courses.prerequisite_text: graduate standing or consent of instructor. (S/U grade only.)

courses.title: Topics in Probability and Statistics
courses.description: Introduction to varied topics in probability and statistics. In recent years, topics have included Markov processes, martingale theory, stochastic processes, stationary and Gaussian processes, ergodic theory. May be taken for credit six times with consent of adviser as topics vary.
courses.prerequisite_text: graduate standing. Nongraduate students may enroll with consent of instructor.

courses.title: Further Topics in Probability and Statistics
courses.description: Continued development of a topic in probability and statistics. Topics include Markov processes, martingale theory, stochastic processes, stationary and Gaussian processes, ergodic theory. May be taken for credit three times with consent of adviser as topics vary.
courses.prerequisite_text: MATH 289A. Students who have not completed MATH 289A may enroll with consent of instructor.

courses.title: Exploratory Data Analysis and Inference
courses.description: An introduction to various quantitative methods and statistical techniques for analyzing data—in particular big data. Quick review of probability continuing to topics of how to process, analyze, and visualize data using statistical language R. Further topics include basic inference, sampling, hypothesis testing, bootstrap methods, and regression and diagnostics. Offers conceptual explanation of techniques, along with opportunities to examine, implement, and practice them in real and simulated data. Recommended preparation: familiarity with linear algebra and mathematical statistics highly recommended.
courses.prerequisite_text: graduate standing. MATH 290A-B-C. Topology (4-4-4) Point set topology, including separation axioms, compactness, connectedness. Algebraic topology, including the fundamental group, covering spaces, homology and cohomology. Homotopy or applications to manifolds as time permits. Prerequisites: MATH 100A-B-C and MATH 140A-B-C.

courses.title: Topics in Topology
courses.description: Introduction to varied topics in topology. In recent years topics have included generalized cohomology theory, spectral sequences, K-theory, homotophy theory. May be taken for credit six times with consent of adviser as topics vary.
courses.prerequisite_text: graduate standing. Nongraduate students may enroll with consent of instructor.

courses.title: Further Topics in Topology
courses.description: Continued development of a topic in topology. Topics include generalized cohomology theory, spectral sequences, K-theory, homotophy theory. May be taken for credit three times with consent of adviser as topics vary.
courses.prerequisite_text: MATH 291A. Students who have not completed MATH 291A may enroll with consent of instructor.

courses.title: Seminar in Topology
courses.description: Various topics in topology. May be taken for credit nine times.
courses.prerequisite_text: graduate standing or consent of instructor. (S/U grade only.)

courses.title: The Mathematics of Finance
courses.description: Introduction to the mathematics of financial models. Hedging, pricing by arbitrage. Discrete and continuous stochastic models. Martingales. Brownian motion, stochastic calculus. Black-Scholes model, adaptations to dividend paying equities, currencies and coupon-paying bonds, interest rate market, foreign exchange models.
courses.prerequisite_text: MATH 180A (or equivalent probability course) or consent of instructor.

courses.title: Special Topics in Mathematics
courses.description: A variety of topics and current research results in mathematics will be presented by staff members and students under faculty direction.

courses.title: Graduate Student Colloquium
courses.description: A variety of advanced topics and current research in mathematics will be presented by department faculty. (S/U grades only.) May be taken for credit six times.
courses.prerequisite_text: graduate standing.

courses.title: Mathematics Graduate Research Internship
courses.description: An enrichment program that provides work experience with public/private sector employers and researchers. Under supervision of a faculty adviser, students provide mathematical consultation services. May be taken up to three times for credit.
courses.prerequisite_text: consent of instructor.

courses.title: Reading and Research
courses.description: Independent study and research for the doctoral dissertation. One to three credits will be given for independent study (reading) and one to nine for research.
courses.prerequisite_text: consent of instructor. (S/U grades permitted.)

courses.title: Honors Linear Algebra
courses.description: First quarter of a very rigorous three-quarter honors integrated linear algebra/multivariable calculus sequence for extremely well-prepared students. Topics include real/complex number systems, vector spaces, linear transformations, bases and dimension, change of basis, eigenvalues, eigenvectors, diagonalization. (Credit not offered for both MATH 31AH and 18.)
courses.prerequisite_text: AP Calculus BC score of 5. Students without an AP Math BC score of 5 may enroll with a prerequisite of MATH 20A-B with a grade of A or better in each. Students who have not completed listed prerequisites may enroll with consent of instructor.

courses.title: Honors Multivariable Calculus
courses.description: Second quarter of three-quarter honors integrated linear algebra/multivariable calculus sequence for well-prepared students. Topics include derivative in several variables, Jacobian matrices, extrema and constrained extrema, integration in several variables. (Credit not offered for both MATH 31BH and 20C.)
courses.prerequisite_text: MATH 31AH with a grade of B– or better, or consent of instructor.

courses.title: Honors Vector Calculus
courses.description: Third quarter of honors integrated linear algebra/multivariable calculus sequence for well-prepared students. Topics include change of variables formula, integration of differential forms, exterior derivative, generalized Stoke’s theorem, conservative vector fields, potentials.
courses.prerequisite_text: MATH 31BH with a grade of B– or better, or consent of instructor.

courses.title: Foundations of Precalculus
courses.description: Introduction to functions and their properties. Polynomial and rational functions. Exponential and logarithmic functions. Trigonometric functions and their properties.
courses.prerequisite_text: Math Placement Exam qualifying score.

courses.title: Precalculus
courses.description: Functions and their graphs. Linear and polynomial functions, zeroes, inverse functions, exponential and logarithmic, trigonometric functions and their inverses. Emphasis on understanding algebraic, numerical, and graphical. (No credit given if taken after MATH 4C, 10A, or 20A.)
courses.prerequisite_text: Math Placement Exam qualifying score or MATH 3B.

courses.title: Precalculus for Science and Engineering
courses.description: Review of polynomials. Graphing functions and relations: graphing rational functions, effects of linear changes of coordinates. Circular functions and right triangle trigonometry. Reinforcement of function concept: exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions. Vectors. Conic sections. Polar coordinates. (No credit given if taken after MATH 1A/10A or 2A/20A. Two units of credit given if taken after MATH 3C.) Three or more years of high school mathematics or equivalent recommended.
courses.prerequisite_text: Math Placement Exam qualifying score, or MATH 3C, or AP Precalculus score of 4 or 5, or AP Calculus AB score (or subscore) of 2.

courses.title: Teaching Assistant Training
courses.description: A course in which teaching assistants are aided in learning proper teaching methods through faculty-led discussions, preparation and grading of examinations and other written exercises, academic integrity, and student interactions. Number of units for credit depends on number of hours devoted to teaching assistant duties. May be taken for credit up to nine times for a maximum of thirty-six units. Must have concurrent teaching assistant appointment in mathematics.
courses.prerequisite_text: consent of adviser. (S/U grades only.)

courses.title: First-year Student Seminar
courses.description: The First-year Student Seminar Program is designed to provide new students with the opportunity to explore an intellectual topic with a faculty member in a small seminar setting. First-year student seminars are offered in all campus departments and undergraduate colleges, and topics vary from quarter to quarter. Enrollment is limited to fifteen to twenty students, with preference given to entering first-year students.
courses.prerequisite_text: none.

courses.title: Learning Sustainable Well-Being: Compassion for Self and Others, a Mathematician’s Perspective
courses.description: This experiential course teaches the art of practicing psychological well-being, based on Eastern and Western approaches (e.g., mindfulness, positive psychology, cognitive therapy, neuroscience, theatre and art), from the perspective of a mathematician. Each week, there is a short lecture on a given topic, combined with workshop-style exercises. Open to all undergraduate students.

courses.title: Introduction to Teaching Math
courses.description: Revisit students’ learning difficulties in mathematics in more depth to prepare students to make meaningful observations of how K–12 teachers deal with these difficulties. Explore how instruction can use students’ knowledge to pose problems that stimulate students’ intellectual curiosity.
courses.prerequisite_text: none.

courses.title: Putnam Seminar
courses.description: Students will develop skills in analytical thinking as they solve and present solutions to challenging mathematical problems in preparation for the William Lowell Putnam Mathematics Competition, a national undergraduate mathematics examination held each year. Students must sit for at least one half of the Putnam exam (given the first Saturday in December) to receive a passing grade. P/NP grades only. May be taken for credit up to four times.
courses.prerequisite_text: AP Calculus AB score of 4 or more, or AP Calculus BC score of 3 or more, or MATH 20A.

courses.title: Independent Study
courses.description: Independent study or research under direction of a member of the faculty.
courses.prerequisite_text: Must be of first-year standing and a Regent’s Scholar.

courses.title: Prehistory and Ancient Foundations
courses.description: This course explores human origins, the development of early forms of social and political organization, the strategies that early societies used to negotiate their physical and social environments, and the appearance of influential cultural traditions across the ancient world (to circa 100 BCE). Topics include the emergence of agriculture, the relationship between nomad and settled, the birth of the city and the expanding human “footprint,” the development of writing, foundational religious and cosmological ideas and narratives, influential models of visual and material culture, and changing forms of social stratification and inequality. Students may not receive credit for both MMW 11 and MMW 11R. Open to Eleanor Roosevelt College (ERC) students only. Must be taken for a letter grade to meet the ERC graduation requirement.

courses.title: Prehistory and Ancient Foundations
courses.description: MMW 11R is a distance education course. This course explores human origins, the development of early forms of social and political organization, the strategies that early societies used to negotiate their physical and social environments, and the appearance of influential cultural traditions across the ancient world (to circa 100 BCE). Topics include the emergence of agriculture, the relationship between nomad and settled, the birth of the city and the expanding human “footprint,” the development of writing, foundational religious and cosmological ideas and narratives, influential models of visual and material culture, and changing forms of social stratification and inequality. Students may not receive credit for both MMW 11 and MMW 11R. Open to Eleanor Roosevelt College (ERC) students only. Must be taken for a letter grade to meet the ERC graduation requirement.

courses.title: Transforming Traditions and Emerging World Communities, circa 100 BCE–1200 CE
courses.description: This course provides a global perspective on the past from circa 100 BCE to circa 1200 CE, examining the emergence of interregional networks and empires and their relationship with the advent and expansion of diverse religious movements, including Christianity, Islam, and Buddhism, as well as cross-cultural contacts and exchanges. The course also explores forms of identity (ethnic, religious, and other); models of inclusion and exclusion; systems of power, hierarchy, and slavery; and the human-environmental relationship. MMW 12 is the first of two writing-intensive courses in the MMW sequence. Students may not receive credit for both MMW 12 and MMW 12R. Open to Eleanor Roosevelt College (ERC) students only. Must be taken for a letter grade to meet the ERC graduation requirement.
courses.prerequisite_text: satisfaction of the Entry Level Writing Requirement.

courses.title: Exploring the Premodern World
courses.description: This course addresses themes and topics from the premodern world (from antiquity to the eighteenth century) and strengthens students’ analytical, research, and writing skills. Students may not receive credit for both MMW 121 and MMW 121R. Open to Eleanor Roosevelt College (ERC) transfer students only. Must be taken for a letter grade to meet the ERC graduation requirement.

courses.title: Exploring the Premodern World
courses.description: MMW 121R is a distance education course. This course addresses themes and topics from the premodern world (from antiquity to the eighteenth century), and strengthens students’ analytical, research, and writing skills. Students may not receive credit for both MMW 121 and MMW 121R. Open to Eleanor Roosevelt College (ERC) transfer students only. Must be taken for a letter grade to meet the ERC graduation requirement.

courses.title: Exploring the Modern World
courses.description: This course addresses specific themes and topics from the modern world (from the eighteenth century to the present) and strengthens transfer students’ analytical, research, and writing skills. Students may not receive credit for both MMW 122 and MMW 122R. Open to Eleanor Roosevelt College (ERC) transfer students only. Must be taken for a letter grade to meet the ERC graduation requirement.

courses.title: Exploring the Modern World
courses.description: MMW 122R is a distance education course. This course addresses specific themes and topics from the modern world (from the eighteenth century to the present), and strengthens transfer students’ analytical, research, and writing skills. Students may not receive credit for both MMW 122 and MMW 122R. Open to Eleanor Roosevelt College (ERC) transfer students only. Must be taken for a letter grade to meet the ERC graduation requirement.

courses.title: Transforming Traditions and Emerging World Communities, circa 100 BCE–1200 CE
courses.description: MMW 12R is a distance education course. This course provides a global perspective on the past from circa 100 BCE to circa 1200 CE, examining the emergence of interregional networks and empires and their relationship with the advent and expansion of diverse religious movements, including Christianity, Islam, and Buddhism, as well as cross-cultural contacts and exchanges. The course also explores forms of identity (ethnic, religious, and other); models of inclusion and exclusion; systems of power, hierarchy, and slavery; and the human-environmental relationship. MMW 12 is the first of two writing-intensive courses in the MMW sequence. Students may not receive credit for both MMW 12 and MMW 12R. Open to Eleanor Roosevelt College (ERC) students only. Must be taken for a letter grade to meet the ERC graduation requirement.
courses.prerequisite_text: satisfaction of the Entry Level Writing Requirement.

courses.title: A Globalizing World: Exchanges, Entanglements, and Exploitation, Thirteenth–Eighteenth Century
courses.description: This course presents a global perspective on the connections, exchanges, and transformations that linked Afro-Eurasia and the Americas during the period from 1200 to 1750 CE. The course examines the nature and consequences of this increasingly connected world. It focuses on spaces of cross-cultural contact and exchange, including the transfer of technologies, ideas, commodities, and customs and their environmental impact; encounters in the form of travel, trade, migration, and invasion; and exploitation through empire, colonization, and slavery, and their manifestation in state violence, intolerance, discrimination, and racism. MMW 13 is the second of two writing-intensive courses in the MMW sequence. Students may not receive credit for both MMW 13 and MMW 13R. Open to Eleanor Roosevelt College (ERC) students only. Must be taken for a letter grade to meet the ERC graduation requirement.
courses.prerequisite_text: MMW 12 or MMW 12R with a grade of D or better.

courses.title: A Globalizing World: Exchanges, Entanglements, and Exploitation, Thirteenth–Eighteenth Century
courses.description: MMW 13R is a distance education course. This course presents a global perspective on the connections, exchanges, and transformations that linked Afro-Eurasia and the Americas during the period from 1200 to 1750 CE. The course examines the nature and consequences of this increasingly connected world. It focuses on spaces of cross-cultural contact and exchange, including the transfer of technologies, ideas, commodities, and customs and their environmental impact; encounters in the form of travel, trade, migration, and invasion; and exploitation through empire, colonization, and slavery, and their manifestation in state violence, intolerance, discrimination, and racism. MMW 13 is the second of two writing-intensive courses in the MMW sequence. Students may not receive credit for both MMW 13 and MMW 13R. Open to Eleanor Roosevelt College (ERC) students only. Must be taken for a letter grade to meet the ERC graduation requirement.
courses.prerequisite_text: MMW 12 or MMW 12R with a grade of D or better.

courses.title: Divergent Paths to the Modern World, Eighteenth–Twentieth Century
courses.description: This course explores divergent paths to modernity between the mid-eighteenth century and World War I. The course examines the influence of “the West” as a hegemonic force that disrupted global connections and forged new ones, changing the social, economic, political, and ecological norms of societies worldwide. The course investigates how groups and individuals around the world adopted, contested, and/or resisted this influence. Students may receive credit for MMW 14 with any one of the following: MMW 14, MMW 14R, or MMW 14GS. Open to Eleanor Roosevelt College (ERC) students only. Must be taken for a letter grade to meet the ERC graduation requirement.
courses.prerequisite_text: MMW 12 or MMW 12R and MMW 13 or MMW 13R with a grade of D or better.

courses.title: Divergent Paths to the Modern World, Eighteenth–Twentieth Century
courses.description: This course explores divergent paths to modernity between the mid-eighteenth century and World War I. The course examines the influence of “the West” as a hegemonic force that disrupted global connections and forged new ones, changing the social, economic, political, and ecological norms of societies worldwide. The course investigates how groups and individuals around the world adopted, contested, and/or resisted this influence. Students may receive credit for MMW 14 with any one of the following: MMW 14, MMW 14R, or MMW 14GS. Open to Eleanor Roosevelt College (ERC) students only. Must be taken for a letter grade to meet the ERC graduation requirement. Program or materials fees may apply.
courses.prerequisite_text: MMW 12 or MMW 12R and MMW 13 or MMW 13R with a grade of D or better. Students must apply and be accepted to the Global Seminars program.

courses.title: Divergent Paths to the Modern World, Eighteenth–Twentieth Century

The course investigates how groups and individuals around the world adopted, contested, and/or resisted this influence. Students may receive credit for MMW 14 with any one of the following: MMW 14, MMW 14R, or MMW 14GS. Open to Eleanor Roosevelt College (ERC) students only. Must be taken for a letter grade to meet the ERC graduation requirement.
courses.prerequisite_text: MMW 12 or MMW 12R and MMW 13 or MMW 13R with a grade of D or better.

courses.title: The Contemporary Era: Conflict and Aspirations in a Globalized World, Twentieth–Twenty-First Century
courses.description: This course explores the sociocultural, economic, and political forces that shaped the twentieth and twenty-first century and contestations over them, with particular focus on the complex interaction between humans and the natural world. It examines the overlapping causes and impact of the global and local conflicts and inequalities that have defined the contemporary era. The course addresses efforts to defend and expand freedom, improve quality of life, and increase transnational cooperation and communication that challenge those hierarchies that perpetuate inequality. The course reflects on what this recent history may mean for our collective future. Students may receive credit for MMW 15 with any one of the following: MMW 15, MMW 15R, or MMW 15GS. Open to Eleanor Roosevelt College (ERC) students only. Must be taken for a letter grade to meet the ERC graduation requirement. Satisfies the Jane Teranes Climate Change Education Requirement.
courses.prerequisite_text: MMW 12 or MMW 12R and MMW 13 or MMW 13R with a grade of D or better.

courses.title: The Contemporary Era: Conflict and Aspirations in a Globalized World, Twentieth–Twenty-First Century

courses.prerequisite_text: MMW 12 or MMW 12R and MMW 13 or MMW 13R with a grade of D or better. Students must apply and be accepted to the Global Seminars program.
